evidence.claim: A forest road links a mill town and a reservoir crossing
evidence.quote: The route crosses Idaho’s tallest bridge–the Dent Bridge, spanning the Dworshak Reservoir–and winds its way through the vast evergreen forests of the Clearwater Mountains.

evidence.claim: a mill town
evidence.quote: developed by Potlatch as a mill town

evidence.claim: The Elk River Backcountry Byway winds through evergreen forest in the Clearwater Mountains and crosses Dworshak Reservoir on Dent Bridge.
evidence.quote: The route crosses Idaho’s tallest bridge–the Dent Bridge, spanning the Dworshak Reservoir–and winds its way through the vast evergreen forests of the Clearwater Mountains.

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho includes it among the state’s scenic byways and gives the one-way drive two hours.
evidence.quote: Time 2 hours one way

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho includes it among the state’s scenic byways
evidence.quote: A variety of scenic, natural, historic, recreational, archeological and cultural experiences can be found on Idaho’s 31 scenic byways.

evidence.claim: The drive has dips and turns, with farmsteads and patches of timber along Wells Bench.
evidence.quote: Travelers quickly enter a series of dips and turns along a rough route that reveals the physical diversity of landscapes in this rural region.

evidence.claim: with farmsteads and patches of timber along Wells Bench
evidence.quote: From Orofino the route begins with a climb up and along Wells Bench where ranchettes and farmsteads are scattered along the benches and between timber patches.

evidence.claim: The reservoir crossing is a two-lane suspension bridge, with a main span of 1,050 feet.
evidence.quote: the two-lane crossing has a main span of 1,050 feet (320 m)

evidence.claim: When Potlatch Lumber Company reached Elk River in 1906, no roads led into the backcountry; logs traveled down the North Fork of the Clearwater during spring runoff.
evidence.quote: When Potlatch Lumber Company came to Elk River in 1906 there were no roads into the backcountry. During spring runoff, the North Fork of the Clearwater River became a waterway used to transport logs to the mills in Lewiston.

evidence.claim: The later construction of Dworshak Dam required a new crossing to preserve vehicle access to Elk River.
evidence.quote: Built in conjunction with the Dworshak Dam by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers during the early 1970s, this bridge provides local access over the flooded river, now Dworshak Reservoir. It replaced a smaller bridge which crossed the river prior to the flooding by the reservoir. Without the bridge, vehicle access from Ahsahka to the small community of Elk River would be blocked off.

evidence.claim: The Army Corps of Engineers built Dent Bridge in place of a smaller bridge over the river.
evidence.quote: Built in conjunction with the Dworshak Dam by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers during the early 1970s, this bridge provides local access over the flooded river, now Dworshak Reservoir. It replaced a smaller bridge which crossed the river prior to the flooding by the reservoir.

evidence.claim: Construction began in December 1969, and materials for the new crossing had to come over winding logging roads. The work required hauling more than 20,000 cubic yards of concrete and 4,150 tons of steel into the backcountry.
evidence.quote: Construction began in December of 1969 and proved to be a sizeable challenge to haul more than 20,000 cubic yards of concrete and 4,150 tons of steel over winding logging roads.

evidence.claim: Start at Bovill and follow Idaho 8 to Elk River, the former sawmill town.
evidence.quote: The byway begins in Orofino at Idaho 7 and the junction of Wells Bench Road, crosses the North Fork of the Clearwater at Dent Bridge, then to Elk River where it joins Idaho 8 to Bovill.

evidence.claim: Near Elk River, the cedar grove is reached from Forest Road 382.
evidence.quote: Elk River Historical Museum, the Morris Cedar grove and Elk River Falls are featured along the byway.

evidence.claim: Near Elk River, the cedar grove is reached from Forest Road 382.
evidence.quote: Located on F.S. Road 382, the Perkins Cedar Grove is one of the few remaining old-growth cedar stands in Idaho.

evidence.claim: Continue toward Dent Bridge and the reservoir, then climb through forest to Wells Bench before descending to Orofino.
evidence.quote: From Orofino the route begins with a climb up and along Wells Bench where ranchettes and farmsteads are scattered along the benches and between timber patches. As the forested areas get more prevalent travelers will drop down towards Dworshak Reservoir, crossing Dent Bridge,

evidence.claim: Elk River’s sawmill had a pond built expressly for its logs.
evidence.quote: Elk Creek Reservoir dates back to 1910 when Potlatch built a dam on Elk Creek to create a “Millpond” to store logs for the new sawmill in Elk River.

evidence.claim: The town had begun as a hunting resort before becoming a lumber town in 1909.
evidence.quote: Elk River began as a hunting resort in what was considered wilderness during the late 1800's. Elk River became a hard working lumber town in 1909

evidence.claim: Potlatch dammed Elk Creek in 1910, creating storage where timber brought by horse skid or sleigh could float, protected from insects and drying.
evidence.quote: Logs were brought by horse skid or sleigh to the pond where they were floated to protect the logs from insects and drying.

evidence.claim: The mill used electric power, and the town grew rapidly after Potlatch opened it.
evidence.quote: The town quickly grew when Potlatch opened one of the largest electric-powered sawmills in the country.

evidence.claim: Its Potlatch sawmill was phased out during the 1930s.
evidence.quote: Formerly the site of a Potlatch sawmill, it was phased out after several decades during the 1930s.

evidence.claim: A three-mile Loop Road follows part of the original railroad grade between Elk River and Bovill, the rail connection that served the sawmill.
evidence.quote: The 3-mile long road is built on a section of the original rail road grade between Elk River and Bovill. The railroad provided a vital transportation link for Elk River's sawmill.

evidence.claim: The giant western redcedar belongs to an old-growth grove reached by Trail 748.
evidence.quote: Trail 748 follows through a shady old-growth cedar grove leading to the Idaho Champion western red cedar tree.

evidence.claim: The tree is 177 feet tall and 18 feet in diameter, with an estimated age of 3,000 years.
evidence.quote: Estimated at 3,000 years old, the red cedar at 18 feet in diameter, and 177 feet tall, is Idaho's largest tree.

evidence.claim: Nearby, Trail 749 makes a three-quarter-mile loop among 500-year-old trees in an 80-acre grove.
evidence.quote: Trail 749, a ¾-mile long trail, loops among 500-year-old trees set in an emerald green 80-acre grove.

evidence.claim: Dent Bridge replaced a river crossing that the new reservoir would flood.
evidence.quote: It replaced a smaller bridge which crossed the river prior to the flooding by the reservoir.

evidence.claim: Completed in 1971, the two-lane suspension bridge measures 1,550 feet overall, with a main span of 1,050 feet.
evidence.quote: Completed 55 years ago in 1971 at a cost of $7,848,950, the two-lane crossing has a main span of 1,050 feet (320 m), and an overall length of 1,550 feet (472 m).

evidence.claim: Its name comes from Charles and Katherine Dent, who owned land on the western side in 1895.
evidence.quote: The bridge takes its name from Charles and Katherine Dent, who in 1895 owned land on the western side of where the bridge now stands.

evidence.claim: The settlement of Dent was razed before the reservoir flooded it.
evidence.quote: The settlement of Dent was razed prior to being flooded by the reservoir.

evidence.claim: Building the new bridge preserved access between the Orofino side of the Clearwater and Elk River.
evidence.quote: The Corps of Engineers carefully weighed the possibilities for getting traffic to Elk River from the Orofino side of the Clearwater River.

evidence.claim: Its site was chosen for terrain that would accommodate both the bridge itself and the roads needed to reach it.
evidence.quote: The exact location was based on the topography most suitable for road access as well as for the bridge construction itself.
